title: Price the false alarms and test the guards
brief: A guard that blocks too much is a quiet outage, and one that blocks too little is a headline. How do you put a price on each error and test a guard before users meet it?

blocks.text: Every guard is a classifier with two error rates

blocks.title: Why most blocks are false alarms
blocks.expr: precision = (recall x base rate) / (recall x base rate + FPR x (1 - base rate))

vars.v: share of harmful requests the guard catches
share of all traffic that is harmful
false positive rate, the share of benign requests the guard blocks

blocks.example: With a 0.5% base rate, 95% recall and a 2% false positive rate, precision is 0.00475 / (0.00475 + 0.0199) = **0.193**. About four in five blocks hit a benign request, even though the guard looks excellent.

items.label: Harmful requests
items.note: Per 100,000 requests at a 0.5% base rate. Illustrative arithmetic, not vendor data.

items.label: Share of blocks that are real

blocks.title: What a guard does when it fires
blocks.intro: The action changes what a false positive costs. Foundry offers annotate and annotate and block for models, and agents support annotate and block only (preview) [[r1]].

options.name: Block
options.summary: Stop the request or the answer.
cons: Every false positive is a failed request
Block cannot tell the user what to change
options.bestWhen: Harm is severe and irreversible, such as unsafe tool actions.
options.avoidWhen: The guard is new or its precision is unmeasured.

options.name: Annotate (shadow mode)
options.summary: Record the verdict and let the content through.
pros: Measures real block rates and false positives with no user impact
Builds the labelled set you need
cons: Harm gets through while you learn
options.avoidWhen: Permanent use on a severe-harm surface.

options.name: Repair
options.summary: Redact, rewrite or correct instead of refusing, for example PII redaction or groundedness correction (preview).
pros: Keeps most of the user's help
Lowers the cost of a false positive
cons: A repair can introduce its own errors
Needs a second check on the repaired text
options.bestWhen: A small part of the content is the problem.
options.avoidWhen: Any residue of the content is unacceptable.

options.name: Escalate to a human
options.summary: Hold the item for review or sample it afterwards.
pros: Feeds labels back to the evaluation set
cons: Adds delay and a staffing cost
Does not scale to every request

blocks.title: Evaluate a guard before users meet it

steps.title: Label
steps.md: Build sets for benign, harmful, borderline and adversarial inputs, per language.

steps.title: Measure
steps.md: Recall and false positive rate per category and language, plus latency p50 and p95.

steps.title: Shadow
steps.md: Annotate only on live traffic and compare verdicts with your labels.

steps.title: Review
steps.md: Sample blocks and misses with humans.

steps.title: Set
steps.md: Choose thresholds per category and surface.

steps.title: Canary
steps.md: Enable blocking for a small share, then widen with alerts.

blocks.caption: What to measure and alert on
head: Metric
Why it matters
Alert when
rows: Recall per category and language on a red-team set
It falls below the agreed floor after any change
False positive rate on benign traffic
It exceeds budget or differs by language
Detects drift, including provider model updates
It moves outside an agreed band overnight
Latency p50 and p95 per guard
Parallel guards add the slowest one
A guard becomes the slowest stage

items.symptom: The block rate doubles overnight and nothing changed on your side.
items.cause: A classifier or service model update moved its decision boundary.
items.fix: Alert on block rate, re-run the labelled set, compare recall and false positives with the last run, and keep a rollback path.

items.symptom: Rephrased or encoded attacks get through.
items.cause: The test set holds only plain attacks. Prompt Shields lists encoding attacks and role-play among its subtypes [[r3]].
items.fix: Add encodings, role-play, conversation mockups and document-borne variants to the adversarial set.

items.symptom: The guard scores well and users in another language complain.
items.cause: Evaluation ran in English only, and several features were tested on English only [[r10]].
items.fix: Slice every metric by language and keep a per-language floor.

items.symptom: Medical or legal vocabulary is blocked.
items.fix: Set thresholds per category and surface, review a sample of blocks, and consider custom categories.

items.symptom: Annotations pile up and nobody reads them.
items.cause: Shadow mode has no owner or review cadence.
items.fix: Assign an owner, sample weekly and set an exit date for shadow mode.

quiz.q: Harmful traffic is 1% of requests. A different guard has 90% recall and a 3% false positive rate. What share of its blocks are real harm (precision)?
quiz.explain: True blocks are 0.90 x 0.01 = 0.009 of traffic and false blocks are 0.03 x 0.99 = 0.0297, so precision is 0.009 / 0.0387 = 0.233. Recall alone says nothing about the user-visible cost, because benign traffic is almost all of the traffic.

quiz.q: The block rate for one harm category doubled overnight. You deployed nothing, and complaints about false positives are rising. What do you do first?
options: Disable the guard until the weekend, then review the complaints
Re-run the labelled set and compare with the last run, checking for a provider update
Raise every threshold to the highest level so that the complaints stop and the block rate settles
Replace the classifier with an LLM judge and relaunch it as a new project
quiz.explain: A sudden shift with no deployment points to a classifier or service update, and only a re-run of your labelled set separates a drift in the guard from a change in traffic. Disabling the guard removes protection, raising every threshold hides real harm, and swapping in a judge is a redesign, not a diagnosis.

quiz.q: Put the steps for evaluating and rolling out a guard in order.
items: Label benign, harmful, borderline and adversarial sets per language
Measure recall, false positives and latency offline
Run in shadow mode on live traffic
Review a sample of blocks and misses with people
Set thresholds per category and surface
Enable blocking for a canary share
quiz.explain: Offline measurement comes before live exposure, and shadow mode comes before blocking so that no user pays for tuning. Thresholds are set after the review, because the review shows where they are wrong, and the canary ends the sequence.

takeaways: At low base rates most blocks hit benign requests, even for a good guard
Shadow mode measures false positives before anyone is blocked
Slice metrics by category and language, and alert on block rate drift
Choose the action by the cost of a false positive: block, annotate, repair or escalate
